description.sr_latin: Kako da reagovaš kao pravi Srbin — iznenađenje, frustracija, oduševljenje.
description.en: How to react like a real Serb — surprise, frustration, excitement, and everything in between.

phrases.context: Your friend says they're moving to Japan next month — react with quick, surprised disbelief.
phrases.notes: 'Stvarno' = really. Tone carries it — genuine surprise or dry sarcasm. One of the most-used reactions.

phrases.context: Your friend claims they ran into a famous actor at the bakery — push back in playful disbelief.
phrases.notes: 'Daj' = give (imperative); the literal sense is long gone. 'Ma' is a dismissive particle — together pure disbelief.

phrases.context: Someone asks if you'd ever go skydiving and the answer is a hard no — shut it down flatly.
phrases.notes: 'Nema' = there isn't (it takes the genitive); 'šanse' = chance. Stronger and flatter than 'Ma daj' — a refusal, not just surprise.

phrases.context: A coworker mentions the deadline got moved up to tomorrow — check that they really mean it.
phrases.notes: Neuter form of 'ozbiljan' = serious, used adverbially. Weightier than 'Stvarno?' — you're genuinely checking they're not joking.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you they finally landed the job — fire back something warm and upbeat.
phrases.notes: Everyday, slightly understated approval. Borrowed via German/English; pronounced 'SOO-per'.

phrases.context: The whole plan lines up without a hitch — react with strong, genuine enthusiasm.
phrases.notes: Neuter of 'odličan' = excellent — also the top school grade (a 5). Warmer and stronger than a plain 'Super'.

phrases.context: Your friend passed the exam everyone said was impossible — tip your hat to the achievement.
phrases.notes: Literally 'every honour' — admiration for something earned, not just nice news. No clean English equivalent.

phrases.context: A friend shows you the clip from their wild weekend trip — react like it's seriously cool.
phrases.notes: Standalone interjection of approval; can also mean 'extra good' as an adjective. Casual, a bit youthful.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you their flight got cancelled for the second time — react to the bad news.
phrases.notes: Literally 'horror' — used as a standalone reaction to genuinely bad news, no exaggeration implied.

phrases.context: You stub your toe hard on the table leg and let out a sharp gut reaction on the spot.
phrases.notes: All-purpose cry for pain, shock, or dismay. Short and sharp for pain, drawn out for exasperation.

phrases.context: The bus is five minutes late yet again — react with maximum theatrical doom over the tiny delay.
phrases.notes: 'Katastrofa' = catastrophe, but everyday speech leans hard on playful exaggeration over small annoyances.

phrases.context: A friend keeps prodding about a topic that just isn't worth it — wave the whole thing away.
phrases.notes: 'Pusti' = let go (imperative of 'pustiti'); with the particle 'ma' it becomes a dismissive 'drop it'.

phrases.context: You open the door to a surprise mess the dog made all over the hallway — let out your shock.
phrases.notes: 'Bože' = vocative of 'Bog' (God); 'moj' = my. Said by everyone for surprise or dismay, religious or not.

phrases.context: Your day piles one small disaster on another and you're worn down — sigh it out in weary overwhelm.
phrases.notes: 'Joj' adds emotional weight — something between 'oh' and 'ugh' — and tips this toward overwhelm rather than plain surprise.

phrases.context: Your friend doubts a story you're telling and you want to stress you're not making it up at all.
phrases.notes: Literally 'my God' (acc + dative 'mi'). An emphasis tag for sincerity, not actually religious.

phrases.context: A friend suggests meeting at seven and you want to lock it in with a quick, casual yes.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it holds/applies' (3sg of 'važiti'). Far more natural than 'okej' for agreeing to a plan.

phrases.context: Your friend lays out their take on something and asks where you stand — tell them you're with them.
phrases.notes: Reflexive verb 'slagati se' = to agree; 'se' is its inseparable reflexive marker. More considered than a snap 'baš tako'.

phrases.context: Someone asks whether you're coming to the party — answer like there was never any doubt.
phrases.notes: 'Naravno' = of course. Can land as genuine or lightly sarcastic depending on delivery.

phrases.context: A friend says out loud the exact point you'd been thinking — snap back that they nailed it.
phrases.notes: 'Baš' = exactly/truly (intensifier); 'tako' = like that. Confirms someone's point rather than just agreeing in general.

phrases.context: A friend keeps apologizing for forgetting to call you back — wave it off and reassure them.
phrases.notes: Literally 'there's no connection' ('veze' is genitive after 'nema'). Everyday way to say 'it's fine, don't worry'.

phrases.context: Someone suggests you were secretly nervous before the talk — reject the idea outright as nonsense.
phrases.notes: Literally 'what kind!' ('kakvi' = what sort, with dismissive 'ma'). Rejects a claim or idea, not just bad news.

phrases.context: A friend gushes thanks for the small favour you did them — shrug it off as no trouble at all.
phrases.notes: 'Ništa' = nothing; 'to' = that. Casually downplays a favour or worry someone is making too much of.

phrases.context: Your friend is dragging their feet and you'll miss the start — nudge them to hurry up already.
phrases.notes: 'Ajde' = come on; 'bre' is an untranslatable emphasis particle. 'Bre' comes from Turkish — drop it in and you sound instantly local.

phrases.context: A friend keeps circling back to the same complaint — say it's genuinely starting to wear on you.
phrases.notes: 'Smara' (3sg of 'smarati') = bores/annoys; 'me' = me (accusative object). Very casual, slangy.

phrases.context: You're stuck waiting around with nothing to do and want to say flatly that you're bored.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it is boring to me' — dative 'mi' makes you the one it happens to, not the cause.

phrases.context: The kids won't stop bickering in the back seat — snap that it has to stop right now.
phrases.notes: 'Dosta' = enough; 'više' = more/any longer. Together a sharp 'that's it, stop now'.

phrases.context: Someone asks you to decide on the spot and you're genuinely unsure — stall while you think it over.
phrases.notes: 'Pa' = well/so, the universal Serbian thinking filler; 'ne znam' = I don't know. Half of conversations open with 'pa'.

phrases.context: A friend presses you for an opinion you simply don't have — shrug the whole thing off offhand.
phrases.notes: Literally 'well, what do I know' ('šta' = what). Feels warmer and more offhand than a flat 'ne znam'.

phrases.context: A friend asks an obvious favour and you happily agree, leaning a little on the playful tone.
phrases.notes: Literally 'how not!' Tone decides everything — wholehearted yes or dripping sarcasm.

phrases.context: Your male friend tells you about the rotten run of luck he's been having — show him you feel for him.
phrases.notes: 'Jadan' = poor/pitiful (masculine here); 'jadna' for a woman. Warm sympathy, can also tease gently.

phrases.context: A friend tells you their car got broken into overnight — react with real sympathy for them.
phrases.notes: Neuter of 'grozan' = terrible/awful. A strong, sincere negative reaction to someone's bad news.

phrases.context: A friend shares that their grandmother passed away and you want to offer your condolences gently.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it is grievous to me' — dative 'mi'. Sympathy, unlike 'izvini', which is an actual apology.

phrases.context: You taste a dish a friend cooked and it's honestly excellent — give understated Balkan praise.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it isn't bad' (negated 'biti' + neuter 'loše'). Understated by design — often quietly high praise.

phrases.context: You bite into the cake a friend baked and it's great — tell them sincerely and directly.
phrases.notes: 'Baš' intensifies what follows; 'dobro' = good (neuter). Sincere and direct, unlike the understated 'Nije loše'.

phrases.context: You watch an unbelievable last-minute goal at the match and shout how wild that just was.
phrases.notes: Literally 'madness', but used positively like English 'insane!' for something amazing.

phrases.context: A friend plays you a track they're obsessed with and you think it's brilliant — say it's top-tier.
phrases.notes: Literally 'peak/top'. Very casual praise, mostly younger speakers.
